Case Study · UX/UI Design Consulting · 2019–2020

Building the
flexible-workspace
platform for
the UAE.

Letswork is the all-in-one platform for discovering and booking great places to work — coworking spaces, meeting rooms, day offices, studios, and office rentals — across the Middle East. I led the end-to-end UX design of the original product ecosystem: a native mobile app, a responsive web platform, and a partner-facing admin console. Today, the product serves 80,000+ members across 25 cities.

02 — The problem

The UAE had the world's densest workspace supply — and no way to access it.

By 2019, Dubai was a magnet for freelancers, remote founders, and business travellers — but flexible-workspace discovery and booking was scattered across WhatsApp threads, walk-in negotiations, and disconnected hotel systems. Five distinct problems each needed solving before the product could exist.

01Problem

Discovery was fragmented and largely word-of-mouth.

A consultant looking for a quiet café in Marina, a meeting room in DIFC, and a private day office in Business Bay had to use three different channels — WhatsApp enquiries, direct hotel calls, screenshot-based confirmations. No single surface to compare options side by side. Pricing rarely visible until you'd committed time to a conversation.

What we heard in research "I spend more time finding the room than I spend in the meeting." — Freelance consultant, Dubai
02Problem

Every space type had its own booking logic.

Coworking was check-in based. Meeting rooms required hourly slots with capacity and amenities. Day offices were half-day or full-day blocks. Studios were equipment-included hourly rentals. Office rentals were multi-day calendar-month commitments. Each system spoke a different language — and any unified product would have to make these five distinct logics feel like one experience.

Design challenge How do you collapse five different booking models into a single mental model — without losing the rules each space type actually needs?
03Problem

Partners had no infrastructure to expose their inventory.

The supply side of the marketplace — hotel café managers, premium coworking operators, office providers — had no tool to publish their spaces, manage real-time availability, or action incoming bookings. Many were tracking bookings in spreadsheets, on paper, or by phone. Without a partner platform, the consumer product couldn't reliably show what was bookable right now.

What we observed A hotel front desk turning away a walk-in customer for a meeting room that was, in fact, available — but the manager couldn't confirm without calling someone.
04Problem

Pricing and commitment models were opaque.

Different venues priced differently — some by the hour, some by membership, some only through quoted enquiries. There was no standard way for a professional to understand "what does this cost me, this week, vs. a membership?" Comparison was impossible. Commitment-anxiety was the default emotional state of the booking.

What we heard in research "I'd commit to a monthly membership if I could see what one month actually looked like in venues." — Remote product manager, Abu Dhabi
05Problem

The audience was mobile-first — the available options were not.

The Letswork user was a freelancer between client meetings, a consultant landing at DXB with a laptop, a remote founder taking the next two hours in a café. They were standing in a lobby, not sitting at a desk. The existing booking surfaces — where they existed at all — were desktop-first hotel pages, PDF brochures, or call-only enquiry forms. None matched the audience's reality.

Insight that shaped the brief Mobile is not a port of desktop. It's the primary surface — and every design decision must defer to the standing, in-transit, two-hands-busy user.
03 — Approach

Three steps from problem to product.

A focused research-to-design process anchored on UAE-specific behaviours, not transplanted Western coworking assumptions.

Step 01 · Discover

Field research across the UAE market.

Interviews and shadowing with freelancers, consultants, remote founders, and business travellers across Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Sharjah — observing how they actually discover and book workspaces today. Parallel conversations with venue partners: hotel managers, coworking operators, office providers.

Step 02 · Define

Mapping five space types to one user journey.

Translating the research into a shared information architecture: how does the discovery → details → schedule → confirm shape stay consistent while the inside of each step adapts to coworking, meeting rooms, day offices, studios, or office rentals?

Step 03 · Design

Co-creating with founders in tight loops.

Weekly working sessions with Letswork's co-founders to calibrate the product's personality, voice, and visual identity. Sprint-based delivery: design → review → iterate, with engineering brought in early to validate booking-logic edge cases.

04 — The solution

Five solutions, mapped one-to-one against the five problems.

Each design decision below traces back to a specific user or operational problem identified in research. Nothing in the product exists because it was a "good idea" — every component answers a question.

01
Solution · solves Problem 01

A unified discovery surface — map and list, one visual language.

A single discovery experience that fuses two ways of finding workspaces — map-first for users navigating by location, and list-first for users scanning by space and vibe. Card anatomy stays constant across both views: the same rating chip, the same status pill ("Open" / "Closed"), the same Check-In CTA.

Five iconographic markers on the map encode space type at a glance, creating a small visual taxonomy that makes the entire region scannable from a single tap. Users can switch views without re-learning the language.

SurfacesMobile · Web
PatternsMap + list toggle, persistent cards
ComponentsMap pins, status pills, rating chip
Solves: Problem 01 — fragmented, word-of-mouth discovery
02
Solution · solves Problem 02

A canonical four-step booking ritual — five logics, one shape.

The booking flow was designed as a four-step canonical ritual: Select Date → Choose Duration or Capacity → Pick Amenities → Confirm. The same four-step rhythm carries every booking on the platform, no matter the space type.

Inside each step, controls adapt to the space being booked: an hourly slot picker for meeting rooms; a capacity slider for studios; a half-day / full-day toggle for day offices; a month-block picker for office rentals. Different inside. Identical outside. Users learn the ritual once and apply it everywhere.

SurfacesMobile · Web
PatternCanonical 4-step flow
Variants5 (one per space type)
Solves: Problem 02 — five booking logics with no shared mental model
03
Solution · solves Problem 03

A partner admin platform built for non-technical operators.

The partner-side admin dashboard was designed with one specific operator in mind: a venue manager with thirty seconds between guests. Every screen had to be operable without training and without the dense data-tables that enterprise SaaS defaults to.

Partners can add and edit space listings, manage real-time availability through a visual calendar, view and action incoming bookings with one-tap accept / decline, and track occupancy and check-ins. Same component vocabulary as the consumer app — recontextualised for an operator audience.

SurfaceWeb dashboard
UserVenue managers, hoteliers
ConstraintZero-training operability
Solves: Problem 03 — partners had no infrastructure to expose inventory
04
Solution · solves Problem 04

A tiered membership system — Daily, Weekly, Monthly, 3-month, Premium.

To resolve commitment anxiety, I designed a clear, comparable tiered membership system — Daily, Weekly, Monthly, 3-Month, plus a Premium tier that unlocks exclusive venues. The plans lead with what you can do, not what you pay; pricing comes second.

Illustrated badges — "Most Popular", "Best Value" — give the founders a flexible commercial lever to test pricing hypotheses without redesigning the screen. The visual hierarchy guides users to the tier that matches their commitment appetite, removing the comparison friction that walk-up workspace pricing had created.

SurfaceMobile · Web
Tiers5 (Daily → Premium)
LeversMerchandising badges
Solves: Problem 04 — opaque pricing and commitment anxiety
05
Solution · solves Problem 05

Mobile-first design from day one — iOS, Android, and full feature parity.

Mobile was the primary surface, not the secondary one. Every interaction was designed for the standing, in-transit user — thumb-zone CTAs, bottom-sheet filters that never leave the user buried in modals, generous tap targets, and a booking flow that completes in three taps from a venue listing.

Both iOS and Android were designed in parallel, with platform-native patterns where it mattered. The responsive web platform, built second, deliberately did not port the mobile design upward. Desktop got desktop-native patterns to serve audiences the mobile app couldn't.

SurfacesiOS · Android · Web
PatternMobile-first, desktop-native web
AudienceStanding, in-transit professionals
Solves: Problem 05 — mobile-first audience, no mobile-first product
Deliverable 01

Mobile App — iOS & Android

The flagship surface. Carries the full weight of discovery, booking, payment, membership, and check-in across all five space types.

iOS · Android
100+ screens
Sequence A

Onboarding & sign-up

A first-run sequence calibrated to the brand voice — illustrated, warm, and instantly clear about what Letswork is before asking for a single tap of intent. UAE-specific country code default (+971) reduces sign-up friction.

Sequence B

Discovery & filtering

Discovery splits between map-first (for users navigating by location) and list-first (for users scanning by space and vibe). Card anatomy holds constant. Filters live in layered bottom-sheets, never full-screen modals — every selection stays visible against the still-scrollable list behind it.

Sequence C

The four-step booking ritual

Date → Duration or capacity → Amenities → Confirm. The same canonical shape carries every booking, regardless of space type. Inside each step, the controls adapt to what's being booked.

Sequence D

Payment & confirmation

The payment screen quiets everything else — one prominent total, two methods, a saved-card affordance that respects returning users. The confirmation screen stops being an app: it tells you you're booked, where to be, and when.

Sequence E

Memberships & account

Plans lead with what you can do, not what you pay. The after-booking experience matters as much as the before: bookings can be amended, cancellations are honest, and the office-rentals flow uses the same canonical ritual the user has already learned.

Deliverable 02

Responsive Web Platform

Full feature parity with the mobile app, engineered for the contexts mobile couldn't serve well — researchers comparing venues, team leads booking off-sites, EAs managing on behalf of executives.

Desktop · Tablet · Mobile Web
Feature-parity surface
Web · Surface A

Home & search

A search-first landing surface tuned for SEO discovery — large brand statement, prominent search composer (city, space type, date), and featured workspace grid. Built so a returning customer could be in a booking flow within two clicks.

Web · Surface B

Discovery — side-by-side map & list

The web platform deliberately did not port the mobile design upward. Desktop got desktop-native patterns: persistent left filter rail, scrolling list in the center, live map on the right. Same brand language, different physics.

Deliverable 03

Partner Admin Platform

The other side of the marketplace. The dashboard used by café managers, hoteliers, and office providers to manage inventory, availability, and incoming bookings — designed for non-technical operators.

Web Dashboard
Two-sided marketplace
Admin · Surface A

Partner dashboard — today at a glance

Designed for a venue manager with thirty seconds between guests. Critical operating metrics surface first — today's bookings, revenue, occupancy, pending approvals — followed by an actionable booking queue with one-tap accept / decline.

06 — Outcome

The brief was UAE-first. What launched became the category-defining regional platform.

Five years on, Letswork is no longer a Dubai start-up. It's the platform 80,000+ professionals open when they need somewhere to work — across the GCC, Iberia, and South Asia. The system designed in 2019 is still the foundational shape of the product.

07 — Reflection

What I'd take into the next one.

The hardest design problems on Letswork were not visual problems. They were structural ones — and they almost never showed up in the screen.

Designing for five booking logics inside one ritual was the central problem. It looked, from the outside, like a UI exercise. It was actually an information-architecture and naming exercise: what is the canonical name of the step where a user picks an hour, a day, a capacity, or a month? Get the naming right, and the screens write themselves.

Two-sided marketplaces are designed twice. The partner admin platform deserved the same design rigour as the consumer app — and the same insight: the operator's workflow is the product, and getting it wrong silently breaks the user-facing experience.

Founder collaboration is its own design surface. Working in tight loops with Letswork's young, creative co-founders meant the work was sharper and the personality of the product was clearer.

Looking at Letswork today — 80,000 members, 500 workspaces, 25 cities — the most satisfying thing is not the scale. It's that the shape we drew in 2019 is still the shape.
